sources.title: J. S. Milne, Lie Algebras, Algebraic Groups, and Lie Groups (course notes, version 2.00)
sources.locator: Chapter I, Section 7 'Root systems and their classification', printed/PDF pp. 66-77: Reflections and Lemmas 7.1-7.3; Definition 7.4 (root system, coroot, integrality); Propositions 7.6-7.13 (Q-form, components, reducedness and multiples, Weyl group simple transitivity, invariant inner product, bases, generation by simple reflections, highest root); the rank-two discussion and Proposition 7.16 with the table of Cartan-integer products (printed pp. 71-73); Theorem 7.18 and the closing list of Dynkin diagrams (printed pp. 74-75); 7.22-7.25 (root lattice, weight lattice, fundamental weights, printed p. 76). Read in the extracted full text.

contents.name: Definition 7.4 and RS3: the root-system integrality axiom and the coroot
Lemmas 7.1-7.3: reflections with a given vector, uniqueness, orthogonal reflection formula
Proposition 7.8 and the reducedness discussion: multiples of a root are +-alpha, or +-alpha/2 and +-alpha in the nonreduced case
Proposition 7.9: the Weyl group acts simply transitively on Weyl chambers
contents.reason: Simple transitivity on chambers is not used by this pair; the finite-type criterion and the classification list supply everything needed for the crystallographic types, and the Weyl group identification here is proved by conjugation of reflections.

contents.name: Proposition 7.10: existence of an invariant inner product on a root system
contents.reason: The existence of invariant inner products for general root systems is not needed: the Coxeter form of the geometric representation is already positive definite under the finiteness hypothesis used on this page.

contents.name: Propositions 7.11-7.12: bases exist, W is generated by the simple reflections, W.S = R
contents.reason: Generation of a Weyl group by its simple reflections is not imported: the theorem proves W(Phi_c) = rho(W) directly from conjugation of reflections and the fact that the r_{a_s} generate rho(W).

contents.name: Proposition 7.16 and the rank-two table (printed pp. 71-73): for distinct simple roots the Cartan-integer pair has product 0, 1, 2 or 3, with angles 90, 120, 135, 150 degrees
Theorem 7.18 and the closing list (printed pp. 74-75): the indecomposable Dynkin diagrams are exactly A_n, B_n, C_n, D_n, E6, E7, E8, F4, G2
7.22: the root lattice Q(R) = ZR and the weight lattice P(R) dual to Q(R^vee), with P(R) containing Q(R)
7.23-7.25: fundamental weights, P(R) = Z.omega_1 + ... + Z.omega_n, dominant weights (printed p. 76)

sources.limits: Reading limit: Milne states at the end of Section 7 that some standard proofs of this section are omitted and refers to Bourbaki, Serre and Casselman; the chapter was used for scope and conventions, not as complete proof evidence for the omitted classification proofs. Knapp and Davis supply those proofs in this batch's reading.

sources.title: Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed. (author-hosted digital second edition, 2023)
sources.locator: Chapter II, Section 5 'Abstract Root Systems', printed pp. 149-162: Proposition 2.48 (multiples of a root; Cartan integers; the Schwarz product bound), Proposition 2.49 (simple roots form a basis with signed integral coordinates), Propositions 2.52-2.54 (abstract Cartan matrices and irreducibility), Lemma 2.56 and pp. 159-162 (reconstruction of the Dynkin diagram from the Cartan matrix); Chapter II, Section 6 'Weyl Group', printed pp. 163-168: Lemma 2.61, Propositions 2.62 and 2.66, Theorem 2.63; Chapter IV, Section 7 'Integral Forms', printed pp. 266-268: Propositions 4.62 and 4.64. Read in the extracted full text.

contents.name: Proposition 2.48(b): the only multiples of a root are +-alpha, and +-2alpha occurs only in a nonreduced system
Proposition 2.48(c) and its proof: the two Cartan integers of nonproportional roots are integers with product at most 3 in absolute value (values 0, +-1, +-2, +-3, with +-4 only for beta = +-2alpha)
Proposition 2.49: simple roots form a basis and every root is a signed integral combination of them
Proposition 2.54, Lemma 2.56 and Figure 2.3 with pp. 159-162: abstract Cartan matrices and reconstruction of the Dynkin diagram from its edge multiplicities
Proposition 2.62: W(Phi) is generated by the simple reflections and every reduced root is a W-image of a simple root
contents.reason: Not needed by this pair: the realization theorem proves W(Phi_c) = rho(W) from conjugation of reflections, and the transfer of the standard root systems is done through the Cartan matrices of the two scalings.

contents.name: Chapter IV, Section 7, Proposition 4.62: an algebraically integral form is integral on the simple coroots
Chapter IV, Section 7, Proposition 4.64: the index of the root lattice in the lattice of algebraically integral forms equals the determinant of the Cartan matrix

sources.title: Michael W. Davis, The Geometry and Topology of Coxeter Groups (first-edition author manuscript, 2007-2008)
sources.locator: Chapter 6, Section 6.9: Theorem 6.9.1 and Table 6.1 of irreducible spherical and Euclidean diagrams, printed pp. 103-104; Appendix C.1: Theorems C.1.2-C.1.4, printed pp. 433-434, including the statement that the classification reduces to positive definiteness of the cosine matrix; the exclusion proof of Theorem C.1.2, printed pp. 434-438. Read in the extracted full text.

contents.name: Table 6.1 and Section 6.9 (printed pp. 103-104): the labelled spherical and Euclidean Coxeter diagrams and the naming conventions for the finite types
Theorem C.1.2 (printed p. 433): the connected positive definite Coxeter diagrams are exactly the list A_n, B_n, D_n, E6, E7, E8, F4, H3, H4, I2(m)
Theorem C.1.3 (printed p. 434): classification of the Euclidean (positive semidefinite of corank one) Coxeter diagrams
contents.reason: The Euclidean semidefinite list is the subject of the later affine classification page of this run; this pair records only the positive definite criterion and never uses the corank-one list.

contents.name: Theorem C.1.4 and Table 6.2: hyperbolic simplicial Coxeter groups of type (n,1)
contents.reason: No item of this pair makes any Lorentzian or hyperbolic statement; the classification input used here stops at the positive definite list, so the hyperbolic table is deliberately not built.

contents.name: The exclusion proof of Theorem C.1.2 (printed pp. 434-438): no cycles, valency bounds and at most one edge of label greater than 3

sources.title: Jean Michel, Lectures on Coxeter groups (Beijing lecture notes, April-May 2014)
sources.locator: Preview of the classification and the definition of Weyl groups, printed p. 3; Section 5 'Classification of finite Coxeter groups', printed pp. 12-15: Proposition 5.14 with proof, the cosine table for m = 2,3,4,5,6, and Theorem 5.15 with its two-part proof including the exclusion steps (i)-(vi). Read in the extracted full text.

contents.name: Printed p. 3: 'A finite Coxeter group is called a Weyl group if it has a reflection representation over Q ... The Weyl groups are the types A, B, D, E, F and G2 := I2(6)', with I2(2)=A1xA1, I2(3)=A2, I2(4)=B2
Proposition 5.14(i)-(ii) (printed pp. 12-13): irreducibility of the reflection representation and the finiteness criterion W finite iff the form is positive definite
The cosine table for m = 2,3,4,5,6 (printed p. 13): -cos(pi/m) and cos^2(pi/m) = 0, 1/4, 1/2, (3+sqrt5)/8, 3/4
Theorem 5.15 with proof (printed pp. 13-15): the finite irreducible list A, B, D, E, F, G, H, I and the exclusion steps (tree, valency, at most one large label, arms)
Remark after the determinant computations (printed p. 14): for types A-G the determinant is the connexion index of the corresponding root system
contents.reason: The connexion-index interpretation of the determinant belongs to algebraic-group theory and is not used; this pair needs only the numerical index [P:Q] = det A in the A2 and B2/C2 examples.

sources.title: J. S. Milne, Lie Algebras, Algebraic Groups, and Lie Groups (course notes, version 2.00)
sources.locator: Chapter I, 7.22-7.25, printed/PDF p. 76: root lattice Q(R) = ZR, weight lattice P(R) as the dual of Q(R^vee), P(R) containing Q(R) with finite quotient P(R)/Q(R), fundamental weights dual to a base of R^vee, and the displayed decompositions Q = Z.alpha_1 + ... + Z.alpha_n, P = Z.omega_1 + ... + Z.omega_n.

contents.name: 7.22: Q(R) = ZR, P(R) = {x : <x, alpha^vee> in Z for all alpha in R}, P(R) contains Q(R) with finite quotient
7.23: fundamental weights omega_alpha defined by <omega_alpha, beta^vee> = delta_{alpha,beta} and forming a basis of P(R)
7.24: dominant weights and the positive cone of the weight lattice
contents.reason: Dominant weights belong to the highest-weight theory of the Lie-theory pages and are not used by either the A page or the examples of this pair.

sources.title: Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed. (author-hosted digital second edition, 2023)
sources.locator: Chapter II, Section 5, Proposition 2.48(c), printed pp. 152-153 (Cartan-integer products for nonproportional roots); Chapter IV, Section 7, Propositions 4.62 and 4.64, printed pp. 266-268 (integral forms and the index of the root lattice in them).

contents.name: Proposition 2.48(c): the product of the two Cartan integers of nonproportional roots is an integer in {0,1,2,3} up to sign, giving cos^2(pi/5) not in {0,1/4,1/2,3/4}
Proposition 4.64: the index of the root lattice in the algebraically integral forms equals the determinant of the Cartan matrix, computed here as 3 for A2 and 2 for B2/C2
Proposition 4.64 applied to the B2 and C2 simple systems

contents.name: I2(4)=B2 among the Weyl types (printed p. 3): the diagram I2(4) is a Weyl type realized by the B2 root system
G2 := I2(6) among the Weyl types (printed p. 3)
H2 = I2(5) is a finite Coxeter type outside the Weyl list (printed p. 3 together with the label-5 exclusion in the proof of Theorem 5.15, printed pp. 14-15)
